_note: Fictional sources for teaching: every source cited here is invented. See sources.json.
title: Plain English, borrowed
context: A law student has paraphrased an abstract about consumer contracts. Compare the paraphrase with the original.
question: Select every phrase in the student's paragraph that is lifted too closely from the original.

sourcePassage.text: Consumer contracts written in plain language are more likely to be read, but readability alone does not guarantee understanding. In a study of 300 consumers, clauses that were easy to read were still frequently misunderstood when they relied on unfamiliar legal concepts.

text: [[x1:Many businesses now promise to write their terms and conditions in plain English.]] [[x2:This is welcome, because long and technical contracts are rarely read at all,]] but [[p1:readability alone does not guarantee understanding]] {{cite:ferreira2020}}. [[x3:Ferreira's study found that]] [[p2:clauses that were easy to read were still frequently misunderstood]] [[x4:by the consumers who took part]] [[p3:when they relied on unfamiliar legal concepts]]. [[x5:Simplifying the wording of a contract]] [[x6:may therefore do little to protect consumers]] [[x7:unless the legal ideas behind the words are explained as well.]] [[x8:Regulators who judge contracts by how easy they are to read]] [[x9:may need to test whether consumers understand them, too.]]

lifted.p1: Six words copied exactly, in the same place in the argument.
lifted.p2: Copied word for word — the longest lifted phrase, and the heart of the source's finding.
lifted.p3: Copied word for word. The sentence around it keeps the original's structure.

feedback.all: You found all three. The student's framing and conclusion are their own, but the middle of the paragraph — the part that reports Ferreira — is stitched together from the abstract's own phrases. That is patchwriting, even with a citation.
feedback.some: You found some of the lifted phrases, but not all of them. Compare the middle of the student's paragraph with the original, phrase by phrase.
feedback.none: These are easy to miss, because the citation makes the paragraph look properly referenced. Compare the middle of the student's paragraph with the original, phrase by phrase.
feedback.falsePositives: Some of the phrases you selected are the student's own. The first two sentences and the last two are the writer's framing and argument — the strongest part of the paragraph.

followUp.question: Which is the best rewrite of 'readability alone does not guarantee understanding'?

options.text: "being readable on its own does not ensure comprehension"
options.feedback: Each word has been swapped for a synonym, but the structure is identical. It's still patchwriting.

options.text: "a contract can be easy to read and still be misunderstood"
options.feedback: Yes. Same meaning, but built from scratch in the writer's own words.

options.text: Keep the words, add quotation marks and a page number.
options.feedback: That would be honest. But nothing about the exact wording matters here, so a real paraphrase is the better choice.

notes.text: In law you will often quote the exact words of legislation or a judgment, because the wording matters. With academic commentary like this, either paraphrase properly or quote — not something in between.

chefsNote: Borrowed phrases are still borrowed, even with a citation.
